slides.title:
6 SEO checks
before you
hit publish
slides.accentLine: Skip one and the page may never rank.

slides.title: One page,
slides.body: Pick one main search term per page. Two pages chasing the same term compete against each other in Google.
slides.action: Write down the main keyword for the page before you write a single word.
slides.example: “Running shoes for flat feet” gets its own page, not a paragraph on “Running shoes”.

slides.title: Keyword first
slides.body: The title tag is the blue link people see in Google. Longer titles usually get cut off after about 60 characters.
slides.action: Put the keyword at the start. Keep the whole title under 60 characters.
slides.example: “Running Shoes for Flat Feet: 7 Picks Tested (2026)”

slides.title: Answer first,
slides.body: ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews pull short, direct answers. Make readers scroll and they skip you.
slides.action: Answer the main question in the first two sentences of the page.
slides.example: “The best running shoes for flat feet have firm arch support and a stable heel.”

slides.title: One H1,
slides.body: Headings are the outline Google reads first. One H1 for the topic, one H2 for every sub-question.
slides.action: Turn the questions people type into Google into your H2 headings.
slides.example: H2: “Do flat feet really need stability shoes?”

slides.title: No page
slides.body: A page with no internal links pointing to it is an orphan page. Google may find it late, or never.
slides.action: Link to the new page from at least 3 related pages on your site.
slides.example: The “Running shoes” category page links to the flat-feet guide.

slides.title: Check it’s
slides.body: Published doesn’t mean indexed. A page that isn’t in Google’s index can’t rank for anything.
slides.action: Google Search Console → URL Inspection → paste the URL → Request indexing.
slides.example: “URL is not on Google” means the page isn’t in the index yet.
